parts.description: Case I: f(x) = k, a constant on [a, b]. Then f'(x) = 0 everywhere on (a, b), so c may be any number in (a, b).
parts.name: case-i-constant

parts.description: Case II: there exists x in (a, b) with f(x) > f(a). By the Extreme Value Theorem (applicable since f is continuous on [a, b] by hypothesis 1), f attains an absolute maximum on [a, b]. Since f(a) = f(b) and the maximum exceeds f(a), the maximum cannot be attained at the endpoints, so it occurs at some c in the open interval (a, b). Then c is a local maximum and, by hypothesis 2, f is differentiable at c. Fermat's Theorem yields f'(c) = 0.
parts.name: case-ii-max-strictly-above-endpoints

parts.description: Case III: there exists x in (a, b) with f(x) < f(a). Symmetric to Case II using the absolute minimum: by EVT f attains an absolute minimum on [a, b], it cannot occur at an endpoint since f(a) = f(b) exceeds the interior value, hence the minimum is at some c in (a, b), c is a local minimum, and Fermat's Theorem yields f'(c) = 0.

parts.description: The three cases are exhaustive: either f is constant on [a, b] (Case I), or there is some interior x with f(x) > f(a) (Case II), or there is some interior x with f(x) < f(a) (Case III). en.text: To find the absolute maximum and minimum values of a continuous function f on a closed interval [a, b]: (1) compute f at the critical numbers of f in (a, b); (2) compute f at the endpoints, f(a) and f(b); (3) the largest of the values from steps 1 and 2 is the absolute maximum; the smallest is the absolute minimum. This procedure is valid because the extreme value theorem guarantees existence of absolute max and min, and every interior local extremum occurs at a critical number (Fermat reformulated).

Este procedimiento es válido porque el teorema del valor extremo garantiza la existencia de máximo y mínimo absolutos, y todo extremo local en (a, b) ocurre en un número crítico (Fermat reformulado).

\begin{aligned}
  \frac{d}{dx}\sin x &= \cos x, &
  \frac{d}{dx}\cos x &= -\sin x, &
  \frac{d}{dx}\tan x &= \sec^{2} x,\\[4pt]
  \frac{d}{dx}\csc x &= -\csc x \cot x, &
  \frac{d}{dx}\sec x &= \sec x \tan x, &

\end{aligned}

en.text: With x in radians, the derivatives of the six trig functions are: (d/dx) sin x = cos x; (d/dx) cos x = −sin x; (d/dx) tan x = sec² x; (d/dx) csc x = −csc x cot x; (d/dx) sec x = sec x tan x; (d/dx) cot x = −csc² x. The minus signs accompany derivatives of the cofunctions.

\frac{d}{dx}\bigl[f(x) - g(x)\bigr] \;=\;

en.text: If f and g are differentiable, then (d/dx)[f(x) − g(x)] = (d/dx) f(x) − (d/dx) g(x).

en.text: Difference rule (derivative)

es.text: Regla de la diferencia (derivada)

latex.body:
f'(a) \text{ exists } \;\Longrightarrow\;
\lim_{x \to a} f(x) = f(a)

en.text: If f is differentiable at x = a, then f is continuous at x = a. The converse is false: there are continuous functions that are not differentiable (for example, f(x) = |x| at x = 0).

theorem.differentiable-implies-continuou.notes: The non-converse remark (|x| at 0) is recorded inside the natural-language statement but is established as fact through proposition.non-differentiability-cases (which uses the |x| example explicitly) and the continuity of |x| from §2.5. en.text: Differentiability implies continuity

es.text: Derivabilidad implica continuidad

latex.body:
f(x) = a^{x},\ a>0,\ f'(0)\text{ exists}
  \;\Longrightarrow\; f'(x) \;=\; f'(0)\cdot a^{x}

en.text: If the exponential function f(x) = a^x (with a > 0) is differentiable at 0, then it is differentiable everywhere and f'(x) = f'(0) · a^x. Hence the rate of change of any exponential function is proportional to the function itself.

es.text: Si la función exponencial f(x) = a^x (con a > 0) es derivable en 0, entonces es derivable para todo x y f'(x) = f'(0) · a^x. En consecuencia, la razón de cambio de cualquier función exponencial es proporcional a la función misma.

theorem.exponential-derivative-proportio.notes: This is Stewart's Eq 4 (page 179). It is a conditional theorem: the conclusion holds IF f'(0) exists. Stewart only provides numerical evidence (table of values) for the existence of f'(0) when a = 2 and a = 3 — he does not prove it. The existence of f'(0) for general a is open debt; flagged in proof.exponential-derivative-proportional.stewart with dependency_confidence:medium. en.text: The derivative of an exponential function is proportional to the function

es.text: La derivada de una función exponencial es proporcional a la función

latex.body: \frac{dy}{dt} = k\,y \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad y(t) = y(0)\,e^{k t}

en.text: The only solutions of the differential equation dy/dt = k y are the exponential functions y(t) = y(0) e^{k t}, where y(0) is the initial value and k is the proportionality constant (k > 0 → growth; k < 0 → decay).

es.text: Las únicas soluciones de la ecuación diferencial dy/dt = k y son las funciones exponenciales y(t) = y(0) e^{k t}, donde y(0) es el valor inicial y k es la constante de proporcionalidad (k > 0 → crecimiento; k < 0 → decaimiento).

theorem.exponential-growth-decay-solutio.notes: Stewart's Theorem 2, §3.8 p. 237. Stewart proves only the forward direction (verification that Ce^{kt} satisfies the ODE) inline; the converse (uniqueness — that EVERY solution has this form) is asserted but its proof is deferred to §9.4. Hence dependency_confidence:medium and an open uniqueness debt for the §9.4 milestone. Newton's law of cooling (dT/dt = k(T − T_s)) and the continuous compound interest formula A(t) = A_0 e^{rt} are derived from this theorem in §3.8 by change of variable / limit; they are pedagogical applications, not new mathematical content, and are not modeled as separate theorem nodes.

f \in C([a,b]) \implies \exists c, d \in [a,b]:\;
f(c) = \max_{[a,b]} f \;\wedge\; f(d) = \min_{[a,b]} f

The proof is explicitly omitted ("aun cuando el teorema del valor extremo es muy aceptable a nivel intuitivo, su demostración es difícil, por consiguiente, se omite") — deferred to Apéndice F. en.text: Extreme Value Theorem

es.text: Teorema del valor extremo

latex.body: \bigl(f \text{ has local extremum at } c\bigr) \;\wedge\; \bigl(f'(c) \text{ exists}\bigr) \;\implies\; f'(c) = 0

en.text: If f has a local maximum or local minimum at c, and if f'(c) exists, then f'(c) = 0.

es.text: Si f tiene un máximo o un mínimo local en c, y si f'(c) existe, entonces f'(c) = 0.

theorem.fermat.notes: Stewart Theorem 4 §4.1 page 276. Stewart explicitly warns (Examples 5, 6) that the converse is false — f'(c) = 0 does NOT imply local extremum (e.g., x³ at 0), and a local extremum can occur where f'(c) does not exist (e.g., |x| at 0). en.text: Fermat's Theorem

es.text: Teorema de Fermat

en.text: If f is continuous on [a, b], then the function g defined by g(x) = ∫_a^x f(t) dt,   a ≤ x ≤ b, is continuous on [a, b] and differentiable on (a, b), and g'(x) = f(x).

theorem.ftc-part-1.notes: Abbreviated TFC1. Discovered by Isaac Barrow (Newton's teacher, ~1670). States that integration and differentiation are inverse operations in one direction: differentiating an area-accumulation function recovers the integrand. The companion TFC2 (theorem.ftc-part-2) handles the other direction: evaluating a definite integral via antiderivatives. en.text: Fundamental Theorem of Calculus, Part 1

es.text: Teorema fundamental del cálculo, parte 1

en.text: If f is continuous on [a, b], then ∫_a^b f(x) dx = F(b) − F(a) where F is any antiderivative of f; that is, F' = f.

theorem.ftc-part-2.notes: Abbreviated TFC2. The central computational theorem of integral calculus: it reduces the hard problem of computing a definite integral (an infinite limit) to the easy problem of finding any antiderivative and evaluating at endpoints. Stewart uses the bracket notation [F(x)]_a^b = F(b) − F(a). Historical note: Isaac Barrow (1670), then Newton and Leibniz independently discovered and exploited this relationship. Multi-source note: Rudin Thm 6.21 states the same result for the Riemann-Stieltjes integral with α(x) = x. Future Rudin Ch6 extraction will extend this node or create a companion. theorem.net-change-theorem is an equivalent restatement emphasising the "integral of a rate = net change" interpretation.

en.text: Fundamental Theorem of Calculus, Part 2

en.text: If F is an antiderivative of f on an interval I, then the most general antiderivative of f on I is F(x) + C, where C is an arbitrary constant.

theorem.general-antiderivative.notes: Stewart §4.9 Teorema 1 page 344. The "+ C" appearing in every indefinite integral and every solution to a first-order ODE in §4.9 / Ch5 / Ch9 is justified by this single result. Stewart's statement implicitly assumes I is an interval (connectedness) — on a disconnected domain (e.g. R \\ {0}) one obtains independent constants on each component, as illustrated by the ln|x| example on the same page.

f \in C([a,b]) \;\text{or } f \text{ has finitely many jump discontinuities}
\;\implies\; \int_a^b f(x)\,dx \text{ exists}

f(a) \neq f(b)
